title: Challenger Deep
sub: Drop Everest in and you still need rope
blurb: The deepest surveyed point on Earth sits at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 metres down. Stand Everest on the bottom of it and the summit would still be more than two kilometres under water.

title: Eight Tonnes on a Thumbnail
sub: A thousand atmospheres, all at once
blurb: At the bottom of the Challenger Deep the pressure is around 1,086 bar — roughly a thousand times what you are under now, and about eight tonnes on every square inch. A polystyrene cup sent down comes back the size of a thimble.

title: The Deepest Fish
sub: And the depth no fish can pass
blurb: A snailfish was filmed at 8,336 metres in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench in 2022. It is close to a hard limit: the chemical that keeps fish cells working under pressure stops being able to do so at about 8,400 metres, and below that the trenches are fishless.

title: Life Without the Sun
sub: A whole world that ignores the surface
blurb: Hydrothermal vents pour out water at up to 400 °C, too pressurised to boil. Nothing here eats sunlight: the base of the food chain is bacteria living on hydrogen sulphide. Until 1977 nobody thought an ecosystem could work this way.

title: Fewer Than the Moon
sub: More people have stood on another world
blurb: Twelve people have walked on the Moon. Fewer than thirty have reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep, eleven kilometres below a boat you could stand on. Space is far away; the deep sea is simply hard.

title: We Have Better Maps of Mars
sub: Most of our own planet is a blur
blurb: Only about a quarter of the sea floor has been mapped at modern resolution. The rest is inferred from satellite gravity measurements, which means whole mountain ranges are drawn as smudges. Mars, the Moon and Venus are all better charted.
stats: Better mapped than our sea floor
